subject: physics
title: Work, kinetic and potential energy
key_idea: Work done is the energy transferred by a force. It equals force × distance moved in the direction of the force. Energy is never created or destroyed, so work done changes kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy by the same amount.

blocks.text: A force does work when it moves something. This section covers the size of the work and its link to energy.

items.meaning: The energy transferred when a force moves an object. It is force × displacement in the direction of the force.
The unit of work and energy. One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force.

blocks.label: Work done
where: θ = angle between the force and the displacement

items: Only the component of the force **along the movement** does work: F cos θ.
If the force is along the movement, θ = 0° and W = Fs.
If the force is at 90° to the movement, W = 0. A force at right angles does no work.
The energy transferred to an object is equal to the work done on it.
Work done = Fs cos θ, in joules.
Only the component of force along the displacement does work.
Energy transferred = work done.

blocks.text: Energy can be transferred from one form to another, but the total stays the same.

items: The **principle of conservation of energy**: energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one form to another.
The total energy of a closed system is constant.
Common forms include kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic, thermal, chemical and electrical energy.
Work done by a force is one way of transferring energy.
Not all energy ends up as useful energy. Some is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy.
Total energy is conserved.
Energy is transferred between forms, for example by work done.

blocks.text: Moving objects have kinetic energy. Raised objects have gravitational potential energy.

blocks.label: Change in gravitational potential energy
where: ΔEₚ = change in gravitational potential energy, in J
g = gravitational field strength, 9.81 N/kg near the Earth's surface
Δh = change in height, in m

blocks.text: The formula for ΔEₚ holds in a uniform gravitational field, so for heights that are small compared with the radius of the Earth.

diagram.alt: A slider showing an object falling from a height. The gravitational potential energy lost equals the kinetic energy gained, so the speed at the bottom depends on the height.

items: When an object falls with no resistive forces, potential energy lost = kinetic energy gained.
Equating them gives ½mv² = mgΔh, so v = √(2gΔh). The mass cancels.
When an object rises, kinetic energy is transferred to gravitational potential energy.
Eₖ = ½mv² and ΔEₚ = mgΔh.
Without resistive forces, potential energy lost equals kinetic energy gained.

blocks.text: Both formulae follow from W = Fs and the equations of motion.

items.text: Lift a mass m slowly through a height Δh. The lifting force equals the weight, F = mg.
This work is stored as gravitational potential energy, so ΔEₚ = mgΔh.
A constant resultant force F accelerates a mass m from rest to speed v over a distance s. F = ma.
From the equations of motion, v² = 2as, so s = v² / 2a.
Work done = Fs = ma × v² / 2a = ½mv².
This work becomes kinetic energy, so Eₖ = ½mv².

items: ΔEₚ = mgΔh comes from W = Fs with F = mg.
Eₖ = ½mv² comes from W = Fs with F = ma and v² = 2as.

checks.q: A rope pulls a sledge 12 m along level ground with a force of 80 N at 30° above the horizontal. Calculate the work done by the rope.
A 0.40 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5.0 m. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed just before it hits the ground.
Show that the work done in lifting a mass m through a height Δh at constant speed is mgΔh.
checks.a: At constant speed the lifting force equals the weight, F = mg. Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force = mg × Δh.

blocks.text: Be ready to use energy conservation both in calculations and in explanations, with work done against resistive forces.

items: If a resistive force R acts over a distance s, the energy transferred to thermal energy is Rs.
For a falling object with air resistance: potential energy lost = kinetic energy gained + work done against resistive forces.
A common method is to find the work done against resistance from the energy that is missing: mgΔh − ½mv².
